name: Manipal End Point
hook: Where Manipal's plateau runs out and the sky takes over.
why: The northern lip of town. Officially it's End Point Park; unofficially, it's where students go for sunset. The Swarna river passes just north of Manipal, so the view falls away to green river country instead of concrete. Ten minutes from Tiger Circle, zero planning, a chai-and-dusk reset.
bestTime: Late afternoon to sunset. Park hours not confirmed online (verify locally).
seasonNote: Clear, dry evenings from October to March give the cleanest sunsets over the Swarna valley. In the monsoon it's green and moody, but the laterite paths get slick.

safety: The plateau edges are laterite and can crumble, so stay behind the railings. Ride back slowly after dark: campus roads are thick with two-wheelers and pedestrians.

name: Manipal Lake (Mannapalla)
hook: The 'muddy lake' that gave Manipal its name and its evening loop.
why: The name is Tulu: Manna Palla means 'muddy lake', and the town is named after it. Today it's a freshwater circle about 500 m across, right in the middle of town, with a boating facility, joggers and students doing laps. Low effort, high mood, next door.
bestTime: Early morning or evening. Boating hours and fees not confirmed online (verify locally).
seasonNote: Works all year. Cool winter mornings are best for a lap; in the monsoon it's full and the path is wet. Boating hours: verify locally.

name: Hasta Shilpa Heritage Village Museum
hook: Eighteen rescued old homes, rebuilt brick by brick in Manipal.
why: An open-air museum of real dwellings moved here from Malnad, the Canara coast and North Karnataka: the Miyar House at the gate, a Mudhol palace Darbar Hall, a 13th-century Harihara shrine. Inside are textiles, utensils, Ganjifa cards, toys and folk deities. Give it two unhurried hours.
bestTime: Weekday mornings. 10 am-5 pm, last ticket 3 pm per Karnataka Tourism or 3:45 pm per Outlook Traveller. Both say closed Mondays and holidays, but a Dec 2025 blog says Tuesdays, so verify locally.
seasonNote: Mostly an outdoor walk between houses, so the dry season is easiest. It works in the rain too, but carry an umbrella. Closed Mondays per Karnataka Tourism (one blog says Tuesday), so verify locally.

name: Udupi Sri Krishna Matha & the Ashta Mathas
hook: Everyone sees Krishna through the same nine holes in a wall.
why: Darshan is through the Kanakana Kindi, a silver window with nine openings in the west wall. Legend says the idol turned to face Kanakadasa, the saint who was kept outside, and there's still no paid queue-jumping. Around the temple sit the eight Ashta Mathas (Palimaru, Admaru, Krishnapura, Puttige, Shirur, Sodhe, Kaniyoor, Pejavara), which take turns running it in two-year Paryayas. Then there's the free leaf-plate meal that made 'Udupi' a word for food.
bestTime: Weekday mornings, roughly 5-7 am, for a quieter darshan (Karnataka Tourism). Around noon for prasada bhojana.
seasonNote: Open year-round. Festival peaks bring crowds: Makara Sankranti and Saptotsava in January, Krishna Janmashtami in August–September, and Paryaya (every two years, January of even years). Go at dawn on a weekday for a quieter darshan.

temple.dressCode: Since 19 Jan 2026 (Shiroor Matha Paryaya, Sri Vedavardhana Tirtha): men must remove shirts and vests (a shawl is allowed) for the WHOLE day inside the Matha premises, and no bermudas. Before this, the shirt-off rule applied only until the afternoon Mahapuja. Women: no half-skirts or bermudas; saree or salwar kameez recommended, no jeans or sleeveless. Footwear outside; no photography in the main shrine.
temple.darshanTimings: Sources differ: 4:30 am-9:30 pm (Karnataka Tourism, trawell.in) or 5 am-9 pm (Wikipedia). Rituals pause the queue briefly. Approximate pujas: Nirmalya Visarjana ~5 am, Mahapuja ~11 am, Ratri Puja ~7:30 pm, Ekanta Seva ~8:50 pm (Wikipedia). Darshan is through the Kanakana Kindi (nine-hole window). One free queue, no paid darshan.
temple.annadana: Free daily prasada bhojana in the Anna Brahma tradition: you sit on the floor and eat off a leaf. Served at noon per Wikipedia. The exact lunch window and any dinner service aren't confirmed by an official source, so verify locally.

bikeTips: Five kilometres from Tiger Circle. Car Street is packed with pedestrians, so park in the lots around Rathabeedi and walk in. Leave shoes and helmets at the stands. Udupi station is about 4 km from the city bus stand if friends come by Konkan Railway.
safety: Crowds, and the stone floors get slippery after washing. Carry little while you're shirtless in the queue. Midday stone can be hot underfoot.

name: Car Street (Ratha Beedi), Udupi after dark
hook: Lamps, chants and palanquins: Udupi's temple square works late.
why: Ratha Beedi is the square around the Krishna Matha, ringed by the Ashta Mathas' own quarters and the Anantheshwara and Chandramouleeshwara temples. Evening rituals run from Ratri Puja (about 7:30 pm) to Ekanta Seva (about 8:50 pm). The child Krishna goes round the temple in a palanquin, and the chariots come out on special occasions. Don't treat it as a sight. Wander between the mathas and let the old town do its thing.
bestTime: Roughly 7-9 pm, between Ratri Puja and Ekanta Seva (Wikipedia; times approximate).
seasonNote: Every night of the year, but the dry season is most comfortable for wandering. Festival nights around Sankranti and Janmashtami are the liveliest and most crowded.

name: Anantheshwara & Chandramouleeshwara Temples, Udupi
hook: Shiva first, then Krishna: Udupi's oldest bit of etiquette.
why: Tradition says you visit these two Shiva shrines before the Krishna Matha, and the Paryaya Swamiji does too. Chandramouleeshwara sits about six feet below street level with a tilted Nandi, so you tilt your head to see the linga. Anantheshwara, credited to the 8th-century Alupas and built in Kerala style, has a 40-ft deepasthambha. Madhvacharya is said to have taught here, and to have vanished from here.
bestTime: Morning, before Krishna darshan. Mondays are busy (Inditales).
seasonNote: Open year-round, right beside the Krishna Matha. Maha Shivaratri (February–March) brings special pujas and crowds.

name: Pajaka Kshetra (Madhvacharya's birthplace)
hook: The village where Madhvacharya was born, still full of his legends.
why: A green village south-east of Udupi, with a small shrine that holds Madhvacharya's footprint. The stories are all around it: the Vasudeva Teertha pond he's said to have made for his mother, and the tamarind tree whose seeds became coins to clear his father's debt. Kunjarugiri hill is a kilometre or two away; legend says he leapt home from it.
bestTime: Morning, combined with Kunjarugiri. Shrine timings not confirmed online (verify locally).
seasonNote: Prettiest just after the monsoon, when the paddy around it is green; pleasant through winter. Hot by April. Shrine timings: verify locally.

name: Kunjarugiri Durga Temple (Durga Betta)
hook: A short stair climb to Durga, with the coastal plain below.
why: A hilltop Durga shrine credited to Parashurama, ringed by four ponds named after his weapons: Dhanus, Gada, Bana and Parashu. The goddess is under two feet tall; the view from the top is huge. Young Madhvacharya is said to have climbed up every day, and his footprints are worshipped in a rock cave.
bestTime: Early morning or late afternoon. Temple hours not confirmed online (verify locally).
seasonNote: Clear post-monsoon and winter days give the long views from the hill. The steps get slippery in the monsoon. Temple hours: verify locally.

name: Kemmannu Hanging Bridge & Hoode backwaters
hook: A wobbly footbridge onto an island in the Swarna backwaters.
why: A narrow suspension bridge (search 'Thimmana Kudru Hanging Bridge') swings out to an island where the Swarna nears the sea at Hoode. Coconut palms, canoes, still water. Kayak operators wait on the far side, and Hoode beach and the Kodi Bengre spit are minutes further on.
bestTime: Morning, or the hour before sunset.
seasonNote: Kayaking runs outside the monsoon, from October to May; calmest and coolest from October to February. In June–September the backwater swells and rentals are mostly shut (verify locally).
bikeTips: Take the Udupi-Santhekatte-Hoode beach road and turn for Kemmannu about 1.5 km before Hoode beach. The last kilometre is narrow, which suits a bike.
safety: Don't crowd or bounce the bridge; its load limit isn't confirmed online, so follow any posted signs. The island has private properties, so stay on the paths. Wear a life jacket if you paddle.

name: Swarna River kayaking (Kemmannu & Thonse-Hoode)
hook: Paddle mangrove channels with egrets, mudskippers and the odd otter.
why: The Swarna's tidal backwaters around Kemmannu and Thonse-Hoode are shallow, slow and lined with mangroves. Expect egrets, herons, crabs and mudskippers, and sometimes otters. Most outfits use double kayaks, with an operator paddling alongside. Thirty minutes is plenty for most people; sessions also run to about 1.5 hours.
bestTime: Early morning or evening (Karnataka Tourism).
seasonNote: Paddle season is October to May, best in the cool early mornings of winter. The Swarna runs high and fast in the monsoon, so don't paddle then.
bikeTips: Ride to the Kemmannu hanging bridge; the put-in is across it. There are no lockers or changing rooms (eNidhi), so leave valuables with the bike.
safety: Life jacket on, always. Keep away from the strong currents near the river mouth and follow the operator's line. Use a dry bag; capsizes happen.

name: Malpe Beach & Sea Walk
hook: Udupi's big beach, plus a promenade walking out to sea.
why: A wide sweep of sand with jet skis, parasailing and banana boats in season. The Sea Walk is about 450 m of promenade with the sea on one side and the Swarna backwaters on the other. You'll find the fisherman-family sculpture there, plus the St. Mary's boats and lamps after dark.
bestTime: Sunset. Main beach 6 am-7 pm; Sea Walk and floating bridge 8 am-6 pm; water sports 9 am-6 pm (Karnataka Tourism; subject to change).
seasonNote: Karnataka Tourism rates October–January best. Water sports restart after the monsoon ban (in 2026 that was 18 September). Monsoon (June–September): rough sea, red flags, no swimming, and boats and water sports stop.
bikeTips: Twelve kilometres, an easy ride via Udupi. Weekend evenings jam up near the Sea Walk, so arrive by 4:30 pm.
safety: Swim only in designated zones near lifeguards; lifeguards and tourist mitras are deployed (News Karnataka, Sept 2026). Never enter the water from the Sea Walk (Karnataka Tourism). The beach is barricaded in the monsoon for rough seas.

name: St. Mary's Island (Thonsepar)
hook: Hexagonal lava columns, ~90 million years old, a short boat ride out.
why: Four small uninhabited islands of columnar basalt, with hexagonal pillars up to about 6 m tall, dated to roughly 85-90 million years. They're a National Geological Monument. The rock looks stacked by an engineer, and the inner beach has palms for shade.
bestTime: The first boats of the morning, before the heat and the crowds.
seasonNote: Ferries from Malpe run roughly October to May (Karnataka Tourism). Morning boats beat the heat, especially from March. Monsoon (June–September): rough sea, red flags, no swimming, and boats and water sports stop.
bikeTips: Distance and ride time are to Malpe beach and the Sea Walk, where you board. Park there and buy tickets at the jetty counter.
safety: Daylight only; no overnight stays. Don't climb the basalt columns: they're protected and sharp-edged. Swim only in designated safe zones. Shade and facilities are scarce, so carry water. Boats are cancelled in rough seas.

name: Kaup (Kapu) Beach & Lighthouse
hook: A 1901 lighthouse on black rocks, open around sunset.
why: The British built this 27 m lighthouse in 1901 on a rock outcrop right above the sand. From the top on a clear evening, the coast runs both ways and the sun drops straight into the sea. Below, a shallow river mouth is good for paddling ankles. Kapu town also has the Hale and Hosa Marigudi shrines.
bestTime: 4-6 pm, when the lighthouse climb is reportedly open (eNidhi, 2022); verify locally.
seasonNote: Clear-sky sunsets from October to March. Monsoon (June–September): rough sea, red flags, no swimming, and boats and water sports stop. Lighthouse climb hours: verify locally.
bikeTips: About 25 min straight down NH66 via Udupi and Katapadi. Bike parking is paid. NH66 has fast trucks and buses, so avoid riding it at night.
safety: The rocks are wet and slippery; stay off the outer ones at high tide. The river mouth turns dangerous at high tide (eNidhi). The lighthouse stairs are narrow and steep. Swim only where police or lifeguards are on duty.

name: Delta Beach (Kodi Bengre)
hook: A thin sand spit where the Swarna finally meets the sea.
why: Ride down a long sand spit, river on one side, sea on the other, until the road gives out. The Swarna estuary is scattered with small kudru islands, fishing boats and birds, and the sunset light is ridiculous. Few facilities, huge views.
bestTime: Sunrise or sunset; October-April is the season (Karnataka Tourism).
seasonNote: October–April is the season (Karnataka Tourism). Monsoon (June–September): rough sea, red flags, no swimming, and boats and water sports stop. The sand spit is exposed and the river mouth is dangerous in the rains.
bikeTips: Go via Santhekatte and Hoode; the Hoode-Kodi Bengre road is narrow (eNidhi). Alternatively, take the ferry or barge from Hangarakatte across the river. It runs daytime only with limited frequency; verify times locally.
safety: Strong currents at the river mouth and estuary, so don't swim there (Karnataka Tourism). Respect the fishing boats and nets. Don't get stranded on the Hangarakatte side after the last ferry.

name: Mattu Beach
hook: Coconut groves, an estuary, and the GI-tagged Mattu Gulla brinjal.
why: A quiet beach near Katapadi, backed by coconut groves, with the Pangala river mouth close by and St. Mary's visible offshore. The fields around grow Mattu Gulla, the round green brinjal with its own GI tag. It's the cure for Malpe's weekend crowds.
bestTime: Sunset (Karnataka Tourism). No posted timings.
seasonNote: Calm and quiet from October to March. Monsoon (June–September): rough sea, red flags, no swimming, and boats and water sports stop.
bikeTips: Off NH66 at Katapadi, then village roads. The map pin is Mattu village (OpenStreetMap); the beach is at the sea end.
safety: Lifeguards may not be on duty (Karnataka Tourism), so don't swim. The estuary has currents. Keep clear of fishing boats.

name: Padubidri Blue Flag Beach
hook: Karnataka's ticketed, swept-clean Blue Flag beach.
why: One of India's first eight Blue Flag beaches, certified in 2020 along with Kasarkod. It's managed sand: watch towers, changing rooms, a garden walking track, solar lights, and a view towards the Hejamadi delta. The certified stretch is fenced, about 1.5 km south of the free main Padubidri beach, so don't mix them up.

train.notes: Wikipedia names Padubidri as the nearest railway station. Train timings and station-to-beach transport not checked; verify locally.

bestTime: Reported open 9 am-6 pm (eNidhi, 2021); verify locally.
seasonNote: Best from October to March. Blue Flag beaches close swimming in the monsoon. Monsoon (June–September): rough sea, red flags, no swimming, and boats and water sports stop. This season's Blue Flag status and fees: verify locally.
bikeTips: Thirty-five minutes down NH66 past Kaup. Stop at Kaup lighthouse on the way back for sunset.
safety: Swim only in designated zones and follow the signage (Karnataka Tourism). NH66 traffic is heavy and fast, so avoid riding back after dark.

name: Brahmavar (and why you'd stop)
hook: Honestly? A highway town. Its value is what's next door.
why: Brahmavar is a taluk town on NH66, and no source checked names a headline sight in the town itself. Its value is location. The Suvarna and Sita rivers form backwaters here before meeting the sea at Hangarakatte, where a ferry crosses to Kodi Bengre. Barkur, the old Alupa capital, is 3 km away, and Mandarthi and Saligrama are short hops.
bestTime: As a pass-through on a Barkur-Mandarthi-Saligrama loop.
seasonNote: Only worth it as a pass-through on the Barkur–Mandarthi–Saligrama loop, which is easiest in the dry months.
bikeTips: Thirteen kilometres north of Udupi on NH66. Turn off for Hangarakatte if you want the ferry to Kodi Bengre (daytime only; verify times).
safety: NH66 junctions here are busy with buses and trucks. Take care at U-turns, especially at night.

name: Barkur, the old Alupa capital
hook: A forgotten capital: Jain pillars, fort ruins, temples in the paddy.
why: Barkur was the Alupa capital, and later a Vijayanagara province. What survives is scattered: the ruined Kattale Basadi Jain complex with a 20-ft monolithic pillar, the Panchalingeshwara temple, the roughly 900-year-old Chowlikere Ganapathy, and fort ruins with posts once used to tie elephants. Archaeology without crowds or signboards.
bestTime: Morning, before the heat. Site timings not confirmed online (verify locally).
seasonNote: Dry, walkable mornings from October to February. The ruins are overgrown and muddy in the monsoon. Site timings: verify locally.
bikeTips: Three kilometres from Brahmavar on the Barkur-Mandarthi road. The lanes between sites are narrow; ask locals for Kattale Basadi.
safety: Ruins are uneven with loose stone, and snakes can be in the long grass. Don't climb on the monuments.

name: Saligrama Guru Narasimha Temple
hook: A yogic Narasimha carved from saligrama stone, right on NH66.
why: Narasimha sits here in yoga posture, calm rather than ferocious, carved in saligrama stone and dated to around the 8th century. The Kota Brahmins of 14 villages treat him as their guru. A Hanuman faces the shrine, and there are two temple tanks: Chakra and Shankha Theertha.
bestTime: Morning darshan.
seasonNote: Open year-round. The Ratharohana (chariot festival) is on Uttarayana Sankranti in mid-January (Wikipedia); check the exact date locally.

name: Mandarthi Sri Durgaparameshwari Temple
hook: Durga's temple, with five Yakshagana troupes of her own.
why: A big village Durga temple in the paddy north of Udupi. It runs five Yakshagana melas, each with about 45 members and its own bus, staging the Ramayana and Mahabharata as devotees' vow offerings. If you've never seen Yakshagana up close, this is its home ground.
bestTime: Morning darshan, then stay for the free afternoon prasadam.
seasonNote: Open year-round. The annual festival is in February. Its Yakshagana mela tours from about November to May.

safety: Narrow rural roads with buses, so ride slowly through villages. Don't ride home sleepy after an all-night Yakshagana; the temple has a 20-room guest house.

name: Karkala: Gommateshwara (Bahubali) & Chaturmukha Basadi
hook: A 42-foot monolith from 1432, and a temple with four front doors.
why: Bahubali stands 42 ft (13 m) on a granite hill. He was installed on 13 Feb 1432 under King Veera Pandya; the Brahmadeva pillar was added in front in 1436. On a nearby rock, the 1586 Chaturmukha Basadi is fully symmetrical: four identical entrances, 108 granite pillars, and life-size Tirthankaras facing every direction. Karkala's lakes, Anekere with its Kere Basadi and Ramasamudra, round off the day.
bestTime: Early morning (Karnataka Tourism). Timings not confirmed online (verify locally).
seasonNote: Cool months make the barefoot granite climb bearable; by April the rock burns underfoot by mid-morning. The steps are slick in the monsoon.

safety: Granite gets very hot by midday and slippery with dew. Some steps are narrow with no railings. No climbing on statues; these are active places of worship.

name: Kodi Beach & Sea Walk (Kundapura)
hook: Walk a kilometre into the sea where five rivers quit.
why: Kundapura's own beach sits where the Panchagangavalli river meets the Arabian Sea, and a breakwater sea walk lets you stroll straight out between river and surf. Tetrapods, fishing lines, a lighthouse nearby and juice stalls at the start make it a proper evening hangout for locals. Go for sunset and stay until the walkway lights come on.

train.notes: Kundapura is a Konkan Railway stop; onward by auto or local bus to Kodi. Station-to-beach distance not verified — verify locally.

bestTime: Late afternoon to sunset, October to March
seasonNote: Late-afternoon sunsets from October to March. Monsoon (June–September): rough sea, red flags, no swimming, and boats and water sports stop.
bikeTips: From Manipal take NH-66 north to Kundapura and turn off onto Kodi road near the town (eNidhi notes Kodi road joins NH-66 near Vinayaka theatre). eNidhi also rates the beach-side road south from Kundapura towards Sasthana, coconut palms on one side and sea on the other, as a scenic alternative ride back.
safety: Do not climb out onto the tetrapods beside the sea walk: they are wet, algae-slick and the gaps between them are deep. The estuary mouth has river and tidal currents, so treat it as a no-swim zone. No lifeguard presence was confirmed online — verify locally.

name: Trasi Beach
hook: A long gold stripe of sand right off the highway.
why: Trasi is a kilometre-long, gently sloping beach that starts the famous Trasi–Maravanthe run where NH-66 hugs the sand. A small rocky islet sits just offshore, and the sunsets line up straight over it. Easy to hit on the way to Kollur or Byndoor without a detour.

train.notes: Karnataka Tourism puts Kundapura railway station about 12 km away; buses run along NH-66.

bestTime: Sunset, October to March
seasonNote: The sun drops straight into the sea from October to March. Monsoon (June–September): rough sea, red flags, no swimming, and boats and water sports stop. NH-66 runs right beside it, so the sea spray and traffic both get worse in the rain.
bikeTips: Straight up NH-66 past Kundapura. Park well off the highway shoulder: this stretch has fast through traffic and long-distance buses, and people stepping off the road to take photos.
safety: Karnataka Tourism calls the water relatively calm, but no lifeguard service was confirmed online and this is the open Arabian Sea. Wade, don't swim, especially near the islet and at low light. Watch traffic when crossing NH-66.

name: Maravanthe Beach
hook: Sea on your left, river on your right, highway between.
why: NH-66 runs on a thin strip of land here with the Arabian Sea on one side and the Souparnika river on the other, which almost touches the sea before swinging away. It is the coast's most famous few hundred metres of road. Ride it slowly at golden hour, then sit on the sand with a tender coconut.

train.notes: Wikipedia names Senapura on the Konkan Railway as the nearest station; few trains stop there, so check the timetable. Kundapura is the bigger alternative with onward buses on NH-66.

bestTime: Sunset, October to March
seasonNote: Clean skies for the sea-and-river view from October to March. Monsoon (June–September): rough sea, red flags, no swimming, and boats and water sports stop. The highway-side stretch is especially rough in monsoon storms.
bikeTips: Trasi and Maravanthe run together on NH-66, around 55 minutes from Manipal. Boat rides on the Souparnika side have been offered outside monsoon (eNidhi). Pull fully off the road for photos: the carriageway is narrow and traffic is fast.
safety: Udayavani reported a youth swept away by strong waves at the Maravanthe beach near the Maraswamy temple (July 2019). Treat it as an open-sea beach: no swimming beyond knee depth, and none at all in rough water or after dark. The biggest everyday danger here is the highway itself, so don't stop or stand on the carriageway.

name: Ottinene Viewpoint (Kshitija Nesara Dhama), Byndoor
hook: A cliff-top deck over the Byndoor river mouth at sunset.
why: A laterite hillock just north of Byndoor looks down on the spot where the Byndoor river slides into the sea, with flat rocks and sand below. The forest department's Kshitija Nesara Dhama on top has an elevated observation deck and a few cottages. Fifteen minutes is enough for the view; stay an hour and walk down to the beach.

train.notes: Karnataka Tourism puts the station about 4 km away; auto from Byndoor town.

bestTime: Sunset, October to March
seasonNote: Dry-season clarity is what this view needs. In the monsoon the sea goes grey and the viewpoint is often clouded in.
bikeTips: Coordinates and ride time are to Someshwara beach at the foot of the Ottinene hillock (the exact viewpoint was not on OpenStreetMap). eNidhi says there are two ways in: ride up to Kshitija Nesara Dhama on top (road paved as of 2021–22), or park at the Someshwara temple and walk up the hill. Entry was Rs 10 per person with a forest-department register entry; no parking fee (eNidhi, 2021–22). Verify the current fee locally.
safety: Stay behind the railings at the cliff edge, especially at dusk. Karnataka Tourism warns that river currents near the estuary are unpredictable, so don't swim at the river mouth. eNidhi reported no toilets or canteen for day visitors at the top. Ride back to NH-66 before full dark if you're not used to the local roads.

name: Kollur Mookambika Temple
hook: Coastal Karnataka's great Devi shrine, below Kodachadri.
why: Mookambika is worshipped here as a linga with Maha Kali, Maha Lakshmi and Maha Saraswathi integrated on its left side, on the south bank of the Souparnika at the foot of the Kodachadri hills. The temple runs free anna prasada for devotees at lunch and dinner. Kollur is also where you hire jeeps for Kodachadri, so it anchors a whole Ghats weekend.

train.notes: About 28–30 km from Kollur (Karnataka Tourism, Wikipedia). Buses and taxis run from Byndoor and Kundapura.

bestTime: Early morning darshan; weekdays are quieter
seasonNote: Open year-round. Navaratri (September–October) and the annual Rathotsava (around March–April; check locally) are the big crowd times. Monsoon brings fog, leeches and landslide closures on the ghat roads. That matters if you continue to Kodachadri.
vegFoodNearby: Temple anna prasada (free temple prasada meal): lunch from about 12 noon, dinner from about 8 pm, per the temple facilities listing — verify locally

temple.dressCode: Traditional is safest. Karnataka Tourism: men in dhoti or formal trousers, women in saree or other traditional wear, modest clothing; footwear left at the counter. Several guides say men remove shirts and vests to enter the inner shrine and should avoid shorts, lungis and caps. Rules on shirts were not confirmed by an official page — verify locally.
temple.darshanTimings: Karnataka Tourism: 5:00 AM to 9:00 PM with short breaks for rituals and alankara. Third-party guides give roughly 5:00 AM–1:30 PM and 3:00–9:00 PM, with about 3:00–5:00 PM as darshan-only. Timings change on festival days. Verify locally.
temple.annadana: Free lunch and dinner served to devotees as prasadam: from about 12 noon and from about 8 pm (temple facilities listing). It can be suspended on special days, e.g. only darshan and no anna prasada on the 25 Oct 2022 solar eclipse (Udayavani). Verify locally.

bikeTips: Manipal–Kundapura on NH-66, then inland via Hattiangadi on the Kundapura–Kollur road; Hattiangadi and Anegudde make easy stops. Fuel up in Kundapura. Ride the last forested stretch in daylight. Kodachadri jeeps are hired in Kollur (see the Kodachadri entry).
safety: Forest-edge roads around Kollur run through Mookambika Wildlife Sanctuary: watch for animals at dawn and dusk and avoid riding them at night. The Souparnika bathing ghats can run fast after rain, so don't go beyond the steps. Leave valuables secure; footwear goes to the counter.

name: Anegudde Sri Vinayaka Temple (Kumbashi)
hook: Hillock Ganesha at Kumbashi, right beside NH-66.
why: This hillock Ganapati shrine at Kumbashi is one of the best-known Ganesha temples in Udupi district. It is one of the seven Parashurama Kshetra mukti sthalas of the coast and finds a mention in Vadiraja Tirtha's Tirtha Prabandha. It's only half an hour from Manipal, which makes it the natural first stop on any northbound ride.
bestTime: Morning, or around the lunch-time anna prasada
seasonNote: Open year-round, and the weather barely matters. Ganesha Chaturthi (August–September) and Sankashti days bring big crowds.
vegFoodNearby: Temple anna prasada (free lunch reported daily; one listing gives 1:00–2:30 pm) — verify locally

temple.dressCode: Not confirmed by an official source. Guides advise modest traditional wear: dhoti for men, saree or salwar for women; Holidify says no sleeveless tops, shorts or short skirts. Verify locally.
temple.darshanTimings: Listings disagree: 5:30 AM–8:30 PM (templesinindiainfo, templesofindia.org), 5:30 AM–9:00 PM (Yatradham), 7:00 AM–8:00 PM (Holidify). Verify locally.
temple.annadana: Free lunch for devotees reported (Wanderlog reviews); one listing gives 1:00–2:30 pm. Not confirmed on an official page — verify locally.

bikeTips: NH-66 north from Udupi; the temple hillock is at Kumbashi just off the highway before Kundapura. Short climb or ride up to the shrine.
safety: Busy NH-66 junction: slow down well before turning in, and watch for buses pulling over.

name: Hattiangadi Siddhi Vinayaka Temple
hook: A Bala Ganesha with loose jata, in an old Alupa capital.
why: On the banks of the Varahi on the Kundapura–Kollur road, Hattiangadi was once Pattinagara, a capital of the Alupa kings. The roughly three-foot saligrama idol is a standing Bala Ganesha with a jata (matted hair) worn loose at the back, which Deccan Herald calls unique in India. There's a dining hall for devotees and an older Lokanatheshwara temple and kalyani just below.
bestTime: Morning or noon puja
seasonNote: Open year-round. An easy stop on the Kollur road in any season.
vegFoodNearby: Temple meals for devotees in the on-site dining hall (Deccan Herald; itslife.in says free food is served) — timings verify locally

temple.dressCode: Not confirmed online — verify locally. Traditional, modest wear is the safe default.
temple.darshanTimings: Not confirmed online — verify locally. A Deccan Herald writer found alankara and puja under way at noon. Office phone listed by itslife.in: 08254 264201.
temple.annadana: Meals served to devotees in the temple dining hall after puja (Deccan Herald); exact times not confirmed — verify locally.

bikeTips: From Kundapura take the Kundapura–Kollur (Shimoga) road east; the village is about 8 km north-east of Kundapura. Combine with Kollur and Kamalashile in one loop.
safety: Narrow state-highway stretches with buses to Kollur. Overtake carefully. The Varahi riverbank can be slippery, so stay off it.

name: Kamalashile Sri Brahmi Durgaparameshwari Temple & Suparshwa Cave
hook: The goddess as a stone linga, a bat cave next door.
why: Here Brahmi Durgaparameshwari is worshipped as a linga, on the banks of the Kubja in thick forest about 35 km from Kundapura. A kilometre away, the pitch-dark Suparshwa cave holds trishakti lingas, a Naga sannidhi under a dome full of bats, and the spring said to become the Kubja. The morning 'salaam pooja' honours Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan's faith in the goddess.
bestTime: Morning, to catch the salaam pooja and do the cave in daylight
seasonNote: Dry months mean a drier cave floor and a calmer Kubja river. In the monsoon the river rises fast; the temple was submerged in a 1968 flood.
vegFoodNearby: Temple annadana in the temple dining hall (listings describe continuous annadana) — timings verify locally

temple.dressCode: Not confirmed online — verify locally. Traditional, modest wear is the safe default.
temple.darshanTimings: 6:00 AM to 8:00 PM per a 2022 travel blog; no official source found. Verify locally. Phone numbers listed by a temple-accommodation site: +91 95915 60809, +91 63644 80126.
temple.annadana: Annadana served to devotees (travel listings); timings not confirmed — verify locally.

bikeTips: Reached via Kundapura and Siddapura side roads; Deccan Herald notes a good road between Kollur and Kamalashile that continues towards the Agumbe ghats. Bring a strong torch for the cave; the DH writer was guided in by a local shopkeeper.
safety: The Suparshwa cave is pitch dark with uneven, damp rock. Go with a local guide and a proper torch, mind your head, and don't disturb the bats. Stay off the Kubja banks when the river is high. Forest roads: no night riding.

name: Arasinagundi (Arishina Gundi) Falls
hook: Kollur's jungle waterfall, but check that it's open.
why: Arasinagundi sits inside Mookambika Wildlife Sanctuary a few km from Kollur, at the end of a 1–2 km walk through dense forest. The name comes from the yellow (arasina) tint of the water where it lands. Access has been restricted after a fatal accident, so this is one you confirm before you ride.
bestTime: September to January, if open
seasonNote: Treat as closed in every season: a July 2024 forest order barred entry after a death, and a 2026 guide says it's permanently shut. Verify locally; don't trespass.

trek.duration: 1–2 km forest walk each way; 2–3 hours round trip (guides)
trek.howToBook: Historically, a permit from the forest-department office (RFO) opposite the Kollur bus stand. Current status may be a full closure — verify locally before going.

bikeTips: Distance and ride time are to Kollur town, the permit office and approach. Coordinates of the falls weren't on OpenStreetMap. Jungle Lodges' Anejhari camp has offered visits here, a sign that it may only be reachable through official channels.
safety: A visitor died here in 2023 while filming near the falls (triphippies). The rocks around the plunge pool are slick and the drop is real. Do not enter without a valid permit: sanctuary rules apply and closures are enforced. Wildlife present; go in daylight only.

name: Koosalli Falls (near Shiroor, Byndoor)
hook: Six cascading tiers, and a real uphill scramble to reach them.
why: A tiered waterfall in rocky forest near Koosalli village, east of Shiroor; Wikipedia gives six drops totalling about 470 feet. You can see it from the road, but the real payoff is the 2–4 km uphill trail to the base. Budget three hours from the parking spot.
bestTime: October to December, while there is still flow and trails are dry
seasonNote: October to December, while there's still flow and the trail is dry. By late January it thins; in the monsoon the trail is dangerous and deaths have been reported.

trek.duration: About 3 hours from the parking spot (90 min up, 30 min at the falls, 1 hour down — eNidhi). Boards disagree: 2 km (govt) vs 4 km (Jaycees) one way.
trek.howToBook: No online booking found. eNidhi saw a forest-department board at the entrance. Access rules and any fee — verify locally.

bikeTips: North on NH-66 past Byndoor to Shiroor, then east on the Todalli road. eNidhi advises navigating to 'Kallanikki Kosalli' on Google Maps, not the falls pin, and parking there. Ride time is to the nearest routable road and is approximate.
safety: eNidhi reports four deaths on this trek so far. The path is narrow and rocky, and the rocks near the falls are slippery even in dry season. Don't climb the tiers or swim in the pools. Go with someone who knows the trail, start before noon, and be out well before dark.

name: Belkal Theertha (Govinda Theertha) Falls
hook: A holy 300-foot drop, earned with ten hard kilometres.
why: A sacred waterfall falling about 300 feet from Korshi Betta into a forest pool inside Mookambika Wildlife Sanctuary, reached via Jadkal and Mudoor village near Kollur. There are no facilities and the trail is rough, but almost nobody makes it here. Bring food from Kollur and start early.
bestTime: October to December
seasonNote: Karnataka Tourism rates October to January as peak: full falls, drier trails, no leeches. Flow drops by late January and much more by March. Monsoon trails are slippery.

trek.duration: 4–5 km one way from the Mudoor trailhead; 3–4 hours round trip (Karnataka Tourism). eNidhi: about 10 km up and down in total, with very slippery rocks.
trek.howToBook: Forest/sanctuary entry fee collected locally (eNidhi saw Rs 100 per person in 2021). No online booking found. Current fee and process — verify locally.

bikeTips: Distance and time are to Mudoor village (the trailhead, per Karnataka Tourism); the falls themselves weren't on OpenStreetMap. Route: Kundapura, Kollur road, Jadkal, Mudoor. Download offline maps because the signal is weak. Carry cash.
safety: eNidhi rates it extreme and not for families: sharp, slippery rock and stream crossings. Don't trek during or right after heavy rain (Karnataka Tourism warns of flash floods). Ask before entering the pool. Hire a local guide from Mudoor, start by 8 AM, and be out by daylight's end. Sanctuary rules apply: no plastic, no fires, no loud music.

name: Hidlumane Falls
hook: Six stacked cascades on the back door to Kodachadri.
why: On the Nittur side of Kodachadri, Hidlumane is a chain of six cascades, each 50–70 feet, in the Mookambika reserve forest. The first fall is about 3 km from the jeep drop-off, and the path up the higher tiers turns into rock and stream scrambling. It is also the halfway break on the Nittur trekking route to the Kodachadri summit.
bestTime: October to February
seasonNote: Comfortable trekking from October to February; the falls thin through January. It's on the Kodachadri–Hidlumane route, which was closed in 2026, so access: verify locally.

trek.duration: About 3 km to the first fall from the jeep drop-off; steeper scrambling to the sixth (Muddie Trails). Plan half a day.
trek.howToBook: Forest checkpost entry on the Nittur side (Muddie Trails: Rs 100, 'keeps changing'). The Kodachadri–Hidlumane trekking route is booked by route on the Aranya Vihaara portal (aranyavihaara.karnataka.gov.in). Current status — verify locally.

bikeTips: Coordinates are the OSM 'Hidlumane Falls trail', so the route figure is to the nearest road (about 2 km off). The road approach is via Nittur (Hosanagara taluk) on the Kollur–Nagara side, over Ghat sections with hairpins. Start early from Manipal.
safety: Upper tiers involve climbing wet rock; stop at the lower falls if you're unsure. The ghat road to Nittur has blind hairpins, buses and morning fog: no night riding. It's a reserve forest with wildlife, so stay on the trail and keep to daylight.

name: Kodachadri (Sarvajna Peetha) — Trek & Jeep Route
hook: The highest peak in Shivamogga district, by jeep or by foot.
why: At 1,343 m, Kodachadri is the highest point in Shivamogga district and a state-declared natural heritage site, and the Mookambika temple sits at its foot. The summit point is Sarvajna Peetha, reached on foot after the jeep track ends. Most people ride a 4x4 jeep up a battered mud track and walk the last stretch; trekkers come from Nittur past Hidlumane Falls.

train.notes: Train to Byndoor, then bus or taxi to Kollur (about 28–30 km), then a jeep to the peak.

bestTime: October to February, early morning
seasonNote: October to February gives the clearest views and the driest track. Both trekking routes were reported closed in May 2026 with no reopening found, so verify locally. Monsoon brings fog, leeches and landslide closures on the ghat roads.

trek.duration: Nittur route about 9–10 km one way, 8–9 hours round trip (Explurger). Jeep track from Kollur/Nittur reaches near the top, then a short walk to Sarvajna Peetha.
trek.howToBook: Trekking permits are booked by route (Hidlumane or Valur) on the Karnataka Forest Department's Aranya Vihaara portal (aranyavihaara.karnataka.gov.in), with ID details and online payment; daily caps apply. Jeeps are hired privately in Kollur or Nittur, with a separate forest entry fee at the checkpost. Fees reported by blogs vary widely and change often — verify locally.

bikeTips: Distance and time are to Kollur, the usual jeep base; you can't ride a private bike to the top (eNidhi, 2021, reported bikes banned on the summit track). Explurger says Nittur jeeps leave around 6 AM and return by late morning, so it's not an on-demand all-day service. Park the bike in Kollur and stay overnight there.
safety: Overnight stays or camping at the peak: not confirmed as allowed. One operator says camping inside Kodachadri forest has been banned since 2015, and blogs describe no facilities (water, first aid, camping) at the top. Plan to stay in Kollur or Nittur. The jeep track is rough and steep; hold on. Fog and wind on the ridges: stay on marked paths away from drop-offs. Don't trek without a valid permit and guide, and don't use unofficial routes when trails are closed.

name: Someshwara Beach (Paduvari, Byndoor)
hook: Byndoor's gentle beach, tucked under the Ottinene hillock.
why: A one-km strip between the mouth of the Byndoor (Sumanavathi) river and the Ottinene hillock, with a small Someshwara Shiva temple on the shore. The Hindu reports it as one of the safer beaches on the coast because the wave action is mild, and the tourism department has been adding pathways, seating and lighting. Do it with the Ottinene viewpoint above.

train.notes: About 4 km away (Karnataka Tourism, Ottinene page); auto from Byndoor town.

bestTime: Late afternoon to sunset, October to March
seasonNote: Calm water and dry evenings from October to March. Monsoon (June–September): rough sea, red flags, no swimming, and boats and water sports stop.
bikeTips: NH-66 north past Kundapura and Maravanthe to Byndoor. Easy to stack with Maravanthe and the Ottinene deck in one evening ride, and with Kollur the same day.
safety: 'Relatively safe' still means open sea: no swimming near the river mouth (Karnataka Tourism warns of unpredictable currents at the estuary) and none after dark. No lifeguard presence confirmed online — verify locally.

name: Gangolli & the Panchagangavalli Estuary
hook: Five rivers, one mouth, and a lost Portuguese trading post.
why: Gangolli sits on a peninsula with the Arabian Sea on one side and the Panchagangavalli on the other, where the Souparnika, Varahi, Kedaka, Chakra and Kubja rivers meet the sea. The Portuguese set up a trading factory here in the 1500s, and Shivappa Nayaka's Keladi forces destroyed their fleet off Gangolli in 1652. It's a working fishing town today. Come for the estuary views opposite Kodi and the history, not for food (the harbour trade is fish).

train.notes: Konkan Railway stop at Kundapura; onward by road. Station distance not verified — verify locally.

bestTime: Late afternoon
seasonNote: Clear skies over the five-river mouth in the dry months. The estuary floods and boats stop in the monsoon.
bikeTips: Gangolli is across the Panchagangavalli from Kundapura. Ride north on NH-66 and loop in. Pair with Kodi beach on the opposite bank for the full estuary view.
safety: Working fishing harbour: watch for trucks, nets and wet, fish-slick surfaces. Don't swim in the estuary: there are river and tidal currents at the mouth.

name: Anejhari Butterfly Camp (Jungle Lodges, near Kollur)
hook: Sleep by the Souparnika, wake up to butterflies and hornbills.
why: A government-run Jungle Lodges camp inside Mookambika Wildlife Sanctuary near Kollur, beside the Souparnika. The butterfly trail turns up species like the Tamil Lacewing, Malabar Tree Nymph and Red Helen, with a chance of Malabar giant squirrel and gaur. Packages include guided treks, and it's the tidy, legal way to base yourself for Kollur and Kodachadri.

train.notes: Byndoor station, then road to Kollur (about 28–30 km); the camp is near Kollur. Exact transfer — verify locally.

bestTime: October to February
seasonNote: Post-monsoon is butterfly season and the nights are cool. Jungle Lodges camps usually shut for the monsoon; verify locally.
bikeTips: JLR says the camp is about 80 km from Udupi, near Kollur; exact coordinates weren't on OpenStreetMap, so distance and ride time are left blank (Kollur is 76 km and 1h 25m from Manipal). Ride in daylight because the last stretch is sanctuary forest.
safety: Inside a wildlife sanctuary: no wandering off at night, follow the naturalists, and wear proper shoes for the treks (JLR asks for them). Riverbank: don't swim in the Souparnika.

name: Sasihithlu Beach (Mulki)
hook: Two rivers, one sandbar, and Karnataka's original surf break
why: The Shambhavi and Nandini rivers meet the sea here, and the shifting sandbars at the mouth shape the waves. This is where Mantra Surf Club started in 2004 and where the Indian Open of Surfing has been held. Come for a lesson in the morning, or just sit on the spit and watch the river and the sea argue.

train.notes: Karnataka Tourism puts Mulki station about 5 km from Mulki beach; take an auto onward. Few trains stop at Mulki, so check NTES/IRCTC. Mangaluru Central is about 23 km away.

bestTime: Nov–Apr for surf (Karnataka Tourism); early morning for lessons, late afternoon for light.
seasonNote: Surf season is November to April (Karnataka Tourism). Monsoon (June–September): rough sea, red flags, no swimming, and boats and water sports stop. Keep clear of the river mouth all year.
bikeTips: NH66 south via Padubidri, then turn west towards Sasihitlu village; the coordinates are Sasihitlu Road (OSM), so follow local signs the last stretch to the sand. Flat, easy ride. Amenities are basic, so carry water (Karnataka Tourism).
safety: Strong currents near the river mouth (Karnataka Tourism). A 23-year-old drowned at Sasihithlu Mooda beach in Aug 2025 after being swept by waves; authorities warn against entering deep water in rough seas. Swim or surf only with a surf school or where lifeguards are posted; don't wade near the delta, at dusk or after a drink. District beach-water restrictions are imposed during the monsoon and after drownings; check for current notices locally.

name: Someshwara Beach (Ullal)
hook: Black rocks, a seaside Shiva temple and waves you watch, not swim
why: A cluster of black boulders called Rudra Paade (Rudra Shile) juts into the surf, and the Someshwara Shiva temple sits right by the shore. Legend says Sage Sukadeva meditated on these rocks. Climb up for sunset, keep your shoes on, and enjoy the spray from a safe height.

train.notes: Karnataka Tourism puts Mangaluru Central about 15 km away; bus, auto or taxi onward via Ullal.

bestTime: Early morning or late afternoon (Karnataka Tourism); low tide shows more of the rocks.
seasonNote: Clear winter sunsets and dry rocks. A looking beach, not a swimming one, in every season. Monsoon (June–September): rough sea, red flags, no swimming, and boats and water sports stop.
bikeTips: NH66 all the way through Mangaluru, cross the Netravati bridge and turn off for Ullal/Someshwara. City traffic through Mangaluru adds time; avoid the evening rush on NH66. Coordinates are Someshwara locality (OSM); the beach is at its western edge.
safety: Swimming is not advised: hidden rocks and strong currents near Rudra Shile (Karnataka Tourism; Wikipedia). A young doctor died in Sept 2023 after slipping off the Rudrapade rocks into the sea. Stay off wet, wave-washed rocks, especially at high tide and after dark. Little shade: carry water and sun protection.

name: Panambur Beach
hook: Mangaluru's busy, lifeguarded beach with ships queuing on the horizon
why: Wide sand, patrol vehicles, lifeguards, and cargo ships waiting off New Mangalore Port. Jet skis, parasailing and boat rides run in season, and the district holds its Karavali Utsav beach festival and an international kite festival here. It is loud and lively, so come for people-watching and sunset, not solitude.

train.notes: Wikipedia gives Surathkal station 6 km and Mangaluru Central 14 km from the beach; auto or city bus onward.

bestTime: Day visitors 8 AM–7 PM (Karnataka Tourism); go for the last two hours before sunset.
seasonNote: Water sports run outside the monsoon. Weekends and holiday weeks get crowded. Monsoon (June–September): rough sea, red flags, no swimming, and boats and water sports stop.
bikeTips: Straight down NH66 past Surathkal; the beach turn-off is just before NMPT. Watch for port trucks and container traffic on this stretch of highway, especially at the Panambur and Baikampady junctions.
safety: Lifeguards and patrol vehicles on duty; sea entry can be prohibited when currents are strong (Karnataka Tourism). Walking on the port breakwater rocks is forbidden (Wikipedia). All water sports are suspended in the monsoon (June 2026 notice). Stay within the flagged swimming zone and leave by 7 PM.

name: Tannirbhavi Beach & Sultan Battery ferry
hook: Take a five-minute river ferry to a calmer Mangaluru beach
why: You can ride to Tannirbhavi via Kuloor bridge, but it is more fun to leave the bike near Sultan Battery and take the small ferry across the Gurupura river. A path through trees then drops you onto a long, quieter stretch of sand with lifeguards. Tannirbhavi Tree Park (15 acres) is next door if you want shade.

train.notes: From Mangaluru Central take an auto (or city bus 16/16A from Statebank, per Wikipedia) to Sultan Battery, then the ferry across the Gurupura river.

bestTime: Oct–Feb (Karnataka Tourism); weekday afternoons are quietest.
seasonNote: October–February per Karnataka Tourism. The Sultan Battery ferry may not run in rough monsoon weather (verify locally). Monsoon (June–September): rough sea, red flags, no swimming, and boats and water sports stop.
vegFoodNearby: Ideal Cafe (Ideal Ice Cream) (pure veg, ~5 km): Neer dosa with the paneer ghee roast, then a gadbad. That's the coast's two big hits, done veg. Opening status: verify locally.
Woodlands Hotel (pure veg, ~6 km): Lunch on a banana leaf with red rice, then goli baje for the road.
bikeTips: By road: NH66 to Kuloor, then the Tannirbhavi road down the spit (watch for port and industrial traffic). By ferry: ride to Sultan Battery in Boloor (OSRM about 62 km, 1h from Manipal), park, and cross on foot. Ferry fare is reported at about ₹15 per person on travel blogs; not confirmed officially, so verify locally.
safety: Lifeguards on duty during the day, but tides change quickly (Karnataka Tourism). Strong waves and currents put Tannirbhavi on the district's monsoon high alert, with water activities suspended in season (June 2026). Swim only in front of lifeguards and not after sunset. The Blue Flag certification has been in progress for years; no official confirmation that it has been awarded.

name: Kateel Sri Durgaparameshwari Temple
hook: Devi on a river islet, and Yakshagana that runs till midnight
why: The shrine sits on an islet in the Nandini river among paddy fields. Kateel's Yakshagana mela now has seven troupes, more than any other organisation, and they play about 180 shows each a season from November to May. Arrive for evening darshan, eat the temple meal, then find where a Kateel troupe is performing that night.

train.notes: Karnataka Tourism puts the nearest railhead about 18 km away; bus or taxi onward. By bike from Manipal is far simpler.

bestTime: Nov–Mar (Karnataka Tourism). Evenings in Yakshagana season (Nov–May).
seasonNote: Open year-round. From about November to May it's Yakshagana season, when Kateel's melas perform nightly across the region.
vegFoodNearby: Temple annadana (free prasada meal, twice daily after the midday and night Mahapooja; templesinindiainfo.com, verify locally)

temple.dressCode: Dress modestly and respectfully (Karnataka Tourism). Traditional wear advised; exact rules not confirmed by the temple online, verify locally.
temple.darshanTimings: Sources differ: 5:30 AM–9:30 PM, Fridays to 10:30 PM (Mangalore Tourism; templesinindiainfo.com); Incredible India lists 5:00 AM–9:00 PM. Mahapooja at 12 noon. Verify locally.
temple.annadana: Annadana twice daily, after the midday and night Mahapooja, with ganji (rice porridge) in the morning (templesinindiainfo.com). Exact serving times not confirmed officially; verify locally.

bikeTips: NH66 south to Mulki, then inland via Kinnigoli to Kateel (state highway). Good roads through villages and paddy. Riding home after a late Yakshagana show means 50 km of dark highway: stay over in Mangaluru or leave before the end.
safety: Village roads are unlit at night and busy with buses on NH66; avoid riding back tired after midnight shows. Watch for bathing ghats on the river around the temple.

name: Polali Rajarajeshwari Temple
hook: A ten-foot goddess shaped from herb-mixed clay
why: The main image is a roughly 10-foot stucco idol, made from clay said to be mixed with medicinal herbs, and an inscription nearby points to a temple here by the 8th century. Every year the festival includes Polali Chendu, a ball game with up to 500 players. On a normal day it is a quiet village temple, which is the point.
bestTime: Morning darshan. The annual festival with Polali Chendu falls around Feb–Apr (dates vary by source); verify locally.
seasonNote: Open year-round. The annual festival with Polali Chendu falls around February–April (dates vary; verify locally).

temple.darshanTimings: Incredible India: 5:30 AM–8:00 PM. Other listings show a midday break (about 8:30 AM–12:30 PM and 5:00–8:30 PM). Verify locally.

bikeTips: Via Mangaluru outskirts towards Kaikamba/Gurupura and on to Polali (OSRM about 72 km). There is an arch at Kaikamba on the Gurupura road (OSM). Rural roads; watch for buses and cattle.
safety: Narrow village roads with sharp bends and private buses. Avoid riding these back roads after dark. Dress code and annadana are not confirmed online; verify locally.

name: Kadri Manjunatha Temple
hook: Shiva, a bronze Lokeshwara and caves on a Mangaluru hill
why: Mangaluru's oldest Shiva temple stands where Buddhist monks once ran Kadarika Vihara, and a bronze Lokeshwara still sits inside. Spring-fed tanks step up the hill behind it, with the laterite Pandava Caves alongside. The car festival is at Makar Sankranti in mid-January.

train.notes: Karnataka Tourism puts the temple about 5 km from the city; auto from either station.

bestTime: Early morning; Car Festival around Makar Sankranti (mid-January) (Karnataka Tourism).
seasonNote: Open year-round. The Car Festival is around Makara Sankranti in mid-January (Karnataka Tourism). Daily puja times reportedly shift from mid-December to mid-January.
vegFoodNearby: Ideal Cafe (Ideal Ice Cream) (pure veg, ~2 km): Neer dosa with the paneer ghee roast, then a gadbad. That's the coast's two big hits, done veg. Opening status: verify locally.
Woodlands Hotel (pure veg, ~1 km): Lunch on a banana leaf with red rice, then goli baje for the road.

temple.dressCode: Modest and respectful dress (Karnataka Tourism). Men in full-length trousers or dhoti are safest; no shorts or beachwear.
temple.darshanTimings: Not officially published; listings vary (about 5:30/6:30 AM–1/2 PM and 4–8/8:30 PM). Puja times reportedly change mid-Dec to mid-Jan. Verify locally.

bikeTips: NH66 into Mangaluru, exit at Kottara/KPT towards Kadri. City traffic; park near the temple base and walk up to the tanks and caves.
safety: Steps to the springs and caves can be slippery and uneven. Keep silence inside the main sanctum. Annadana not confirmed online; verify locally.

name: Kudroli Shree Gokarnanatha Kshetra
hook: Narayana Guru's 1912 temple, built for those kept out
why: Built in 1912 under Sri Narayana Guru's guidance for the Billava community, who were then kept out of other temples. The Chola-style gopuram dates from 1991 and blazes with colour, and the complex has a Navagraha chamber with murals. During Navaratri this is the centre of Mangaluru Dasara.

train.notes: About 2.5–3 km from Mangaluru Central (trawell.in); short auto ride.

bestTime: Morning or evening puja. Navaratri (Mangaluru Dasara, September–October) is the spectacle; any other time is calm.
seasonNote: Open year-round. Mangaluru Dasara at Navaratri (September–October) is the spectacle and the crush. Come any other time for a calm evening puja.
vegFoodNearby: Ideal Cafe (Ideal Ice Cream) (pure veg, ~1 km): Neer dosa with the paneer ghee roast, then a gadbad. That's the coast's two big hits, done veg. Opening status: verify locally.
Woodlands Hotel (pure veg, ~2 km): Lunch on a banana leaf with red rice, then goli baje for the road.

temple.dressCode: Modest dress, shoulders and knees covered; traditional wear recommended; no shorts or sleeveless tops (trawell.in).
temple.darshanTimings: Listings differ: 6 AM–1 PM and 4–8:30 PM (trawell.in); Incredible India gives 6 AM–9 PM. Verify locally.

bikeTips: NH66 into the city, then via Ladyhill/Urva towards Kudroli. Narrow old-town lanes and parking is tight on festival days.
safety: Heavy city traffic and crowds at evening pujas. Annadana not confirmed online; verify locally.

name: Mangaladevi Temple (Bolar)
hook: The goddess who gave Mangaluru its name
why: The city takes its name from Mangaladevi, and her temple in Bolar is traditionally dated to the 9th century and the Alupa king Kundavarman. It is Kerala-style, with a two-storey gateway and a raised sanctum. On the tenth day of Navaratri devotees haul her chariot through the streets.

train.notes: Bolar is about 3 km southwest of the city centre (Wikipedia); a short auto ride from Mangaluru Central.

bestTime: Morning or evening darshan. Navaratri and the annual Rathotsava are the crowded times.
seasonNote: Open year-round. Navaratri (September–October) and the annual Rathotsava draw big crowds.
vegFoodNearby: Ideal Cafe (Ideal Ice Cream) (pure veg, ~2 km): Neer dosa with the paneer ghee roast, then a gadbad. That's the coast's two big hits, done veg. Opening status: verify locally.
Woodlands Hotel (pure veg, ~3 km): Lunch on a banana leaf with red rice, then goli baje for the road.

temple.darshanTimings: Wikipedia gives 6 AM–1 PM and 4–8:30 PM (another section of the same article says 6–10 AM, 12–1 PM, 4–8 PM). Verify locally.

bikeTips: Through Mangaluru city towards Bolar/Jeppu, near the Netravati side of town. Parking is limited in the lanes.
safety: City traffic. Dress code and annadana are not confirmed online; verify locally.

name: Ananthapura Lake Temple
hook: A shrine in a spring-fed lake, and a crocodile back again
why: Kerala's only lake temple sits in a 302-foot-square tank fed by springs, linked to shore by a narrow footbridge. It is held to be the original seat of Ananthapadmanabha. Babiya, the 'vegetarian' crocodile, died on 9 Oct 2022. A new, smaller one was first reported in Nov 2023 and was filmed on the bank in June 2024; locals call it Babiya-3.

train.notes: Incredible India puts Kasaragod station (KGQ) about 14–15 km from the temple; taxi or auto onward. Trains from Udupi to Kasaragod run via Mangaluru; check NTES/IRCTC.

bestTime: Oct–Mar (Incredible India). Morning session for the light on the lake.
seasonNote: October–March (Incredible India) for cool mornings and a full tank. Open all year; the monsoon is lush but wet.

temple.dressCode: Traditional wear advised; sources disagree on whether men must remove shirts. Not confirmed officially; verify locally.
temple.darshanTimings: 5:30 AM–12:30 PM and 5:30–7:30 PM (Kerala Tourism; hindu-blog.com). Closed during eclipses; times change for major rituals.

bikeTips: NH66 through Mangaluru and Talapady into Kerala, then inland from Kumbla to Ananthapura (OSRM about 105 km, 1h 55m). Carry your licence and vehicle papers when crossing into Kerala.
safety: Do not feed, call or approach the crocodile. Stay on the footbridge and steps and away from the water's edge. Long NH66 ride with heavy truck and bus traffic; avoid riding back after dark.

name: Bekal Fort
hook: A keyhole-shaped laterite fort with its feet in the sea
why: Shivappa Nayaka of Keladi built this 40-acre fort in the mid-17th century, and the walls still drop straight into the Arabian Sea. Climb the central observation tower for a 360° view of surf, beach and coconut palms. Then find the old water tank with its steps and the tunnels.

train.notes: Incredible India lists Bekal Fort station (BFR) as nearest. Only some trains stop there; Kasaragod and Kanhangad are bigger stops. Check NTES/IRCTC.

bestTime: Oct–Mar (Kerala Tourism). Open 8:00 AM–5:30 PM daily (Incredible India); go after 3 PM for the light.
seasonNote: October–March (Kerala Tourism). The laterite ramparts are exposed and slippery in the monsoon, and summer afternoons are fierce.
bikeTips: The longest ride in this region: NH66 through Mangaluru, Kasaragod and on to Bekal (OSRM about 125 km, 2h 15m). Start early, cross Mangaluru before the morning rush, and carry papers for the Karnataka–Kerala border.
safety: Laterite walls and bastions have long unfenced drops to rocks and sea; keep kids close and stay off parapets. Heat and glare at midday: carry water. Riding back 125 km after dark on NH66 is a bad idea; consider an overnight in Kasaragod or the train.

name: Saavira Kambada Basadi, Moodbidri
hook: A thousand carved pillars, and no two alike
why: Built in 1430 by the local chieftain Devaraya Wodeyar, this is the finest of Moodbidri's 18 basadis. Its pillars are all carved differently, and an eight-foot panchaloha Chandraprabha sits in the shrine. A 50-foot manastambha stands out front. Walk on to Guru Basadi, with its 12th-century palm-leaf Dhavala texts, and the carved wooden pillars of the Chowta palace.

train.notes: No rail line to Moodbidri; Mangaluru Junction is about 34 km away (mangaloretourism.in). Ride or take a bus.

bestTime: Morning or late afternoon. Listed hours vary: 7:30 AM–6 PM (mangaloretourism.in) vs 9 AM–8 PM elsewhere; verify locally.
seasonNote: Open year-round. Cool mornings from October to February make the walk between basadis a pleasure. The Moodbidri Kambala is held in the Kambala season (November–March).

temple.dressCode: Modest clothing; footwear off before entering (india-guide.in). Verify locally.
temple.darshanTimings: 7:30 AM–6:00 PM daily (mangaloretourism.in); other listings say 9 AM–8 PM. Verify locally.

bikeTips: OSRM routes inland via Karkala (about 50 km). Watch for private buses on blind bends.
safety: Respect Jain temple customs: no leather inside, quiet in the shrine, ask before photographing. Entry is free according to mangaloretourism.in, but one listing shows a fee; verify locally.

name: Pilikula Nisargadhama
hook: Zoo, 3D planetarium and a Tulu landlord's house in one campus
why: The Pilikula Biological Park holds over 700 animals, including Asiatic lions, dholes and gharials. Next door, the Swami Vivekananda planetarium has an 18 m tilted dome and claims India's first active 3D show in 8K. The heritage village has a restored Guthu Mane, a nagabana and a kambala track, and a 5-acre lake has boating.

train.notes: Pilikula is about 10 km from Mangaluru (Karnataka Tourism); taxi or bus onward from either Mangaluru station.

bestTime: Tue–Sun mornings. Closed Mondays (Karnataka Tourism; Central Zoo Authority).
seasonNote: Cool mornings, when the animals are active. Closed Mondays all year. Monsoon visits work but the grounds are wet.
bikeTips: NH66 to Mangaluru, then inland via Kuloor–Vamanjoor (OSRM about 67 km). Large parking area at the main gate, where the central ticket counter sells tickets for all attractions.
safety: Closed Mondays. Stay behind zoo barriers and follow the zoo's do's and don'ts. Section timings and fees are not consistently published: Karnataka Tourism says 10 AM–5 PM, the official contact page says 10 AM–5:30 PM, and the zoo is listed as 9:30 AM–5:30 PM. Boating hours are not published. Verify locally (zoo: 0824-2263300).

name: Mangaluru city (by train or bike)
hook: Two stations, a fleet of autos, and Mangaluru in a day
why: Mangaluru has two main stations six kilometres apart: Mangaluru Central (MAQ) at Hampankatta, the terminus, and Mangaluru Junction (MAJN) at Padil, once called Kankanadi. Take the train down, then autos between Kudroli, Mangaladevi, Kadri, St Aloysius Chapel and Sultan Battery. Finish with sunset at Tannirbhavi or Someshwara.

train.notes: Central is the city terminus (Matsyagandha Express starts/ends here). Junction (Padil) links the Konkan, Hassan–Mysuru and Malabar lines; some Konkan trains start or end there. The two are about 6 km apart, so check which one your Udupi train uses on NTES/IRCTC. Central is closer to Kudroli, Mangaladevi and St Aloysius; Junction is closer to Kadri and Pilikula.

bestTime: Weekdays, any season; start early, because temples break at midday.
seasonNote: Works year-round; the train dodges NH-66 traffic in any weather. Navaratri (Dasara), Christmas and Kadri's January Car Festival are the busiest times.
vegFoodNearby: Ideal Cafe (Ideal Ice Cream) (pure veg, ~<1 km): Neer dosa with the paneer ghee roast, then a gadbad. That's the coast's two big hits, done veg. Opening status: verify locally.
Woodlands Hotel (pure veg, ~1 km): Lunch on a banana leaf with red rice, then goli baje for the road.
bikeTips: If riding: NH66 via Surathkal and Kuloor. The city stretch from Kottara to Pumpwell is the slow part, especially in the evening rush. Park once and use autos inside the old town.
safety: Busy city roads and NH66 truck traffic; avoid the 5–8 PM rush. Check which station your return train leaves from: missing it because you went to the wrong one is easy.

name: Sultan Battery (Boloor)
hook: Tipu's black-stone watchtower, guarding the Gurupura river mouth
why: Tipu Sultan built this squat black-stone tower in Boloor to stop warships slipping up the Gurupura river; it is now an ASI-protected monument. Climb up for the river view, and peer at the locked underground magazine. The Tannirbhavi ferry leaves from just below.

train.notes: About 5 km from Mangaluru Central (trawell.in); auto or city bus 16/16A.

bestTime: Late afternoon, then the ferry across for sunset at Tannirbhavi.
seasonNote: Daylight visits in the dry months. The Tannirbhavi ferry from here may pause in rough monsoon weather.
vegFoodNearby: Ideal Cafe (Ideal Ice Cream) (pure veg, ~3 km): Neer dosa with the paneer ghee roast, then a gadbad. That's the coast's two big hits, done veg. Opening status: verify locally.
Woodlands Hotel (pure veg, ~3 km): Lunch on a banana leaf with red rice, then goli baje for the road.
bikeTips: NH66 into Mangaluru, then via Urva/Boloor to the riverside. Park here and take the ferry to Tannirbhavi on foot.
safety: Take care on the steps and the open top of the tower. The area around is quiet at night. Timings: sources conflict; entry is reported free. Verify locally.

name: St Aloysius Chapel paintings
hook: Every surface painted by one Italian Jesuit
why: On Lighthouse Hill, the St Aloysius College chapel is covered in Antonio Moscheni's work from the late 19th century. There are about 600 m² of wall frescoes and 400 m² of oil-on-canvas ceiling, every inch of it saints, cherubs and trompe-l'oeil. Walk in from the noise of Hampankatta and look up.

train.notes: On Lighthouse Hill in the city centre; short auto ride from Mangaluru Central. Distance not verified; verify locally.

bestTime: Weekday daytime; visiting hours not published online, verify locally.
seasonNote: An indoor stop that works in any weather. Around Christmas there are services, so go when no Mass is on. Hours: verify locally.
vegFoodNearby: Ideal Cafe (Ideal Ice Cream) (pure veg, ~<1 km): Neer dosa with the paneer ghee roast, then a gadbad. That's the coast's two big hits, done veg. Opening status: verify locally.
Woodlands Hotel (pure veg, ~<1 km): Lunch on a banana leaf with red rice, then goli baje for the road.
bikeTips: Up Lighthouse Hill Road from Hampankatta. Park on campus only if allowed.
safety: It is a working college chapel: dress modestly, keep quiet, and ask before taking photos. Visiting hours, entry fee and photography rules are not confirmed online; verify locally.

name: Chandragiri Fort (Kasaragod)
hook: A ruined laterite fort where the Payaswini meets the sea
why: Another of Shivappa Nayaka's 17th-century forts, this one sits on a 46 m hill above the Chandragiri (Payaswini) river, which once divided Tulunadu from Kolathunadu. It's in ruins now: eight bastions, a trench, a tunnel and cannon-pocked walls. You go for the sunset over the river mouth.

train.notes: About 4–6 km from Kasaragod town (Holidify; Wikipedia); auto or bus onward. Public transport to the fort is thin.

bestTime: Late afternoon to sunset. Holidify lists 8 AM–5:30 PM; verify locally.
seasonNote: Clear skies make the river-mouth view worth the climb. The laterite is slippery in the monsoon.
bikeTips: NH66 to Kasaragod, then a short hop south towards Melparamba. Carry documents for the Kerala border.
safety: Ruined walls, uneven laterite and unfenced drops; watch your footing and don't climb the bastions. The site is isolated, so don't linger after dark. Entry fee (Holidify: ₹5 Indians) and hours unconfirmed by the State Archaeology Department online; verify locally.

name: Madhur Madanantheshwara Siddhivinayaka Temple
hook: A Ganesha temple with a three-tiered elephant-back roof
why: Officially it's Shiva's temple, but the south-facing Ganapathi gets the attention. The gajaprishta roof rises in three tiers like an elephant's back, and the walls carry wooden carvings of Ganesha and Ramayana scenes. It stands on the Madhuvahini (Mogral) river, and its famous Moodappam seva covers the idol in appam.

train.notes: About 7 km from Kasaragod town (Wikipedia); auto or bus onward.

bestTime: Morning darshan; combine with Ananthapura, which is nearby.
seasonNote: Open year-round. Dry, bright mornings show off the roofline. Pair it with Ananthapura.

temple.annadana: Appam offerings (Moodappam seva, Sahasrappa) are distributed as prasada (Wikipedia); no confirmed annadana meal. Verify locally.

bikeTips: NH66 to Kasaragod, then inland to Madhur (OSRM about 112 km, 2h). Carry papers for the Kerala border.
safety: Dress code and darshan timings are not confirmed online either; verify locally. Long NH66 ride: start early, don't ride back after dark.

name: Dharmasthala Shri Manjunatha Swamy Temple
hook: A Shiva temple run by a Jain family that feeds thousands daily.
why: Gates open at 4 am, and by noon the queue complex is a slow river of devotees shuffling toward Manjunatha. Then you walk across to Annapoorna, a kitchen built to feed 30,000 to 70,000 people a day, and eat a free meal on the floor beside strangers. Few places show Tulunadu's mix of Shaiva worship and Jain stewardship this plainly.

train.notes: No railway station near Dharmasthala in the sources checked; ride or take a bus.

bestTime: Weekday mornings, right at 6:30 am darshan, or the 5 pm evening session. Avoid weekends and festival days if you hate queues.
seasonNote: Open year-round. Laksha Deepotsava (around Karthika Amavasya, November–December) is the biggest event and the biggest crowd; weekends are always busy. Monsoon brings fog, leeches and landslide closures on the ghat roads. That applies if you continue up Charmadi.
vegFoodNearby: Annapoorna dining hall (temple annadana, free veg meal, inside the temple complex): lunch 11 am–2:30 pm, dinner 7–10 pm

temple.dressCode: Men must remove shirt and vest before entering the sanctum. Men in half-pants and women in nighties are not allowed in for darshan. No bags inside, no mobile phone use in the temple, children under 2 not allowed in the sanctum.
temple.darshanTimings: 6:30 am–2:30 pm (darshan pauses around 12:00–12:15 pm for Mahapooja and Nithyabali; the afternoon line closes at 2:30 pm or when the queue ends) and 5:00–8:30 pm. Gates open 4 am. Timings may change on special days.
temple.annadana: Free meals at Annapoorna dining hall, 11 am–2:30 pm and 7–10 pm. Annadana begins after Maha Naivedya (11:30 am). Breakfast is served in the queue line on crowded days.

bikeTips: About 97 km via Karkala and Belthangady, roughly 1h 50m. Park only in the allotted parking slots (temple rule). Leave the riding jacket and bag with the bike or at your room: bags are not allowed inside.
safety: Heavy crowds on weekends and festival days; keep valuables close, as the temple itself warns. Use the police-aid posts if you get separated from your group. Do not ride back late at night on the Belthangady–Karkala stretch if tired.

name: Ratnagiri Bahubali, Manjusha Museum & Vintage Car Museum, Dharmasthala
hook: A 39-foot Bahubali, old cameras, and Gandhi's car in one afternoon.
why: The 39-foot monolithic Bahubali on Ratnagiri hill was dragged 64 km from Karkala on a 64-wheel trolley in 1970, and installed in 1982. Twenty minutes of steps gets you a view over the whole temple town. Down below, Manjusha is a magpie's dream of coastal heirlooms, cameras and nutcrackers, and the car museum keeps every vehicle in running order, including one Gandhi travelled in.
bestTime: Bahubali hill in the morning (the temple itself recommends mornings to dodge heat and humidity); museums before or after the noon darshan break.
seasonNote: Ratnagiri hill is best in the clear, cooler months, in the morning. The museums are indoors and fine any time.
vegFoodNearby: Annapoorna dining hall (temple annadana, free veg meal, about 1 km away): lunch 11 am–2:30 pm, dinner 7–10 pm
bikeTips: The statue is about 1 km from the Manjunatha temple, by steps (around 20 minutes) or by road. Opening hours from the official site: Bahubali hill 7 am–6:30 pm; Manjusha Museum 9:30 am–5:30 pm; Vintage Car Museum 8:30 am–1 pm and 2–7 pm.
safety: Midday sun on the open hilltop is harsh; there are shelters and drinking water at the top. Steps can be crowded on holidays.

name: Sowthadka Shri Mahaganapati Temple
hook: Ganapati under the open sky, no walls, no roof.
why: Legend says Ganapati asked the farmers not to build him a temple so nobody would ever face restrictions here. So the idol sits out in a meadow, open to the sky and hung with bells offered by devotees whose wishes came true. Come for the appa prasada and keep an eye on the monkeys.
bestTime: Morning, pairing it with Dharmasthala (about 16 km away).
seasonNote: An open-air Ganapati, so it works year-round. The annual Mahapuja is reportedly in January (verify locally).
vegFoodNearby: Temple prasada meal (served to devotees, per the Dharmasthala official site; timing not confirmed, verify locally)
Appa and laddu prasada sold at temple counters

temple.dressCode: Not confirmed online. Yatradham suggests traditional or formal clothes. Verify locally.
temple.darshanTimings: Not confirmed online; sources conflict. The idol is open-air and described as open round the clock, while listed timings range from about 5–6 am to 7:30–10 pm. Verify locally.
temple.annadana: The temple serves a prasada meal to devotees (Dharmasthala official site). Timing not confirmed online; verify locally.

bikeTips: About 3 km from Kokkada, off the Dharmasthala–Kukke road (SH37); entrance arch is on the highway. Around 16 km from Dharmasthala, so do both in one ride.
safety: Monkeys around the shrine snatch food and prasada; keep bags zipped. The highway stretch near Kokkada carries pilgrim buses.

name: Kukke Shri Subrahmanya Temple
hook: The serpent god's seat, with Kumara Parvatha looming overhead.
why: Kukke sits on the Kumaradhara river with Kumara Parvatha rising behind it, and it is where Karnataka comes for naga rituals like Ashlesha Bali and Sarpa Samskara. Men strip to the waist in the darshan line, priests chant through Ashlesha Bali shifts, and the free annadana keeps going through lunch and dinner. It's also the base camp for the state's most famous trek.

train.notes: Subrahmanya Road station is about 12 km from the temple (Karnataka Tourism). It is not on the Konkan line, so from Udupi you would change at Mangaluru. Train times not checked; verify locally.

bestTime: Weekday mornings. Saturdays, Sundays and November–December festival days are very crowded.
seasonNote: Open year-round. Champa Shashti (November–December) is the peak festival with huge crowds; weekends are always busy. Monsoon brings fog, leeches and landslide closures on the ghat roads.
vegFoodNearby: Temple annadana (free veg meals, inside the temple complex): lunch from 11:30 am to 2 pm, dinner 7:30–9:30 pm

temple.dressCode: Men remove shirt and vest before joining the darshan line; dhoti or white pancha for sevas such as Ashlesha Bali and Sarpa Samskara. Women: saree, churidar or salwar with dupatta, or other modest wear. Shorts and sleeveless tops are not appropriate.
temple.darshanTimings: Sources differ. Commonly listed as about 6:30 am–1:30 pm and 3:30–8:00/9:00 pm, closed roughly 1:30–3:30 pm. Timings change on special occasions; verify locally.
temple.annadana: Free lunch 11:30 am–2 pm and free dinner 7:30–9:30 pm (two non-official sources agree); hours may shift on festival days. Sarpa Samskara is a two-day seva: register in advance and attend both days with photo ID.

bikeTips: About 164 km, roughly 2h 45m. The last stretch from Dharmasthala via Kokkada (SH37) passes Sowthadka. Stay the night if you're doing a seva or the trek.
safety: Huge crowds on weekends and festival days. Don't swim in the Kumaradhara when the current is strong. The approach roads are forest roads, so avoid riding after dark.

name: Kumara Parvatha Trek (Kukke Subramanya route)
hook: One of Karnataka's toughest treks, now permit-only and no camping.
why: From Kukke the trail climbs out of the Kumaradhara valley through forest and grassland to a 1,712 m summit. Old trip reports describe it as a two-day epic with a night at Bhattara Mane, but that's gone. It's now a single, brutal day, booked online, with a strict exit time. If the Kukke side stays shut, the Beedahalli route from the Kodagu side is the shorter way up.

train.notes: About 12 km from Kukke (Karnataka Tourism); not on the Konkan line, change at Mangaluru. You'd need the night before in Kukke to make an early start.

bestTime: October–November post-monsoon; the trek is closed in the monsoon and in summer fire season.
seasonNote: October to December is the realistic window: closed in the monsoon and in fire season. In 2026 only the Beedahalli route reopened (18 Oct); the Kukke route was still shut, so verify locally. Book on Aranya Vihaara.
vegFoodNearby: Kukke temple annadana (free veg meals): lunch 11:30 am–2 pm, dinner 7:30–9:30 pm

trek.duration: Kukke round trip about 20–22 km, roughly 11–12 hours, in a single day. Beedahalli round trip about 14 km, 7–8 hours. Kukke side: 5:30 am start and 6 pm exit were reported for last season; this season's times are not confirmed.
trek.howToBook: Online only via the Karnataka Forest Dept Aranya Vihaara portal (aranyavihaara.karnataka.gov.in). Book 1–30 days ahead. Carry the original ID used to book. Cancellations 8+ days out get a 50% refund, within 7 days nothing (rules effective 15 Jul 2026). Daily cap: 150/day for Kukke (minister, Mar 2026). Portal showed 300 slots/day for Beedahalli in Nov 2026. Fee about ₹350 reported in Dec 2025; confirm on portal. No overnight stay or camping, including at Bhattara Mane/Girigadde. Plastic and paper banned.

bikeTips: Distance is to Kukke Subramanya (trailhead side). The Beedahalli checkpost (Kodagu side) is about 208 km, 3h 40m from Manipal. Sleep in Kukke the night before; you need to be at the gate before dawn. Don't plan to ride back the same evening after a 12-hour trek.
safety: Overnight stays and camping inside the sanctuary are banned; plan to be out by the exit time. Long, steep, exposed sections, so carry 3+ litres of water and food in steel containers. Plastic and paper are banned. Bhattara Mane meal service is not confirmed for 2026, so don't count on it. Leeches in the lower forest early in the season. Don't trek alone, and don't attempt it without a valid permit.

name: Gadaikallu (Jamalabad Fort)
hook: Tipu's rock fortress, reached by 1,876 steps cut into granite.
why: Gadaikallu is a bald granite thumb you can see from the Belthangady road. Tipu Sultan fortified it in 1794 and named it after his mother; the British took it five years later.
